title: KAVACH
subtitle: Pre-execution action firewall for AI agents
explanation: KAVACH sits between an agent and the tools that change the world. title: Problem Statement
subtitle: An agent can turn untrusted content into an unauthorized real-world action.
explanation: A legitimate request such as summarising an inbox can expose the agent to instructions planted in an email. The same failure occurs when an invoice email substitutes a bank account, or a narrow CRM request becomes a broad write. KAVACH evaluates each proposed call with the actual request, source labels and business facts. Success requires showing the connector outcome, not trusting the agent’s final message.

title: Proposed Solution
subtitle: Check intent, authority, argument origin and impact at the tool boundary.
explanation: The input includes a tool name, arguments, trusted request, caller identity and prior outputs. Provenance labels the arguments; consequence analysis stages SQL and file changes or predicts external effects. Policy rules impose denial or human approval. The intent gate and risk signal can add caution. Every decision has an explanation and receipt; safeguarded local execution is separate from merely approving an externally executed call.

title: Architecture & Technical Design
subtitle: One decision engine; execution guarantees depend on the integration path.
explanation: The agent or orchestrator enters through REST, the demo MCP endpoint, a full MCP proxy or framework hooks. The gateway combines manifest, provenance, consequence, policy, intent and risk. In owned execution it calls the environment and connectors with snapshots or delivery windows. In proxy and hook mode the external host executes, so KAVACH does not claim its own undo. Receipts, persistence and telemetry surround both paths. This is a stateful single-writer reference deployment, not a verified horizontally scalable service.

title: Decision path: from call to effect
subtitle: A decision, an execution, and a delivery outcome are separate facts.
sources: kavach/gateway.py: check, execute, resolve_hitl, settle; receipts.py
explanation: A session establishes caller and request; outputs are registered as the task reads. A call is validated against the tool manifest, traced and staged. Deterministic floors precede the final verdict. A model score cannot remove a policy requirement. The decision receipt is written before execution. Allowed local calls execute with their actual safeguard; escalations wait for approval; denials return a replan hint. Connector and delivery results produce subsequent records. A queued email is not a delivered email.

title: Provenance & policy: what is trusted
subtitle: Business records supply facts. Emails and web content do not supply authority.
explanation: Values copied or lightly disguised in emails remain untrusted, including normalized addresses. A user-named document may require confirmation instead of immediate denial; naming a source is not blanket authority. Separate rules ask a person about outbound destinations after untrusted reads, cover destinations with insufficient output context, and accept designated user-only arguments only when the user supplied them. Per-task totals prevent splitting a large operation into small calls. These are implemented checks with residual inference limits, not a proof that arbitrary transformed values are tracked.

title: Consequences & the real limits of undo
subtitle: The deck names the safeguard and who actually arms it.
explanation: SQL and supported file actions run on copied state to produce a diff. Their supported local execution uses a snapshot or row-level change record for undo. Email and payment impact is predicted from typed inputs and records; KAVACH can delay delivery or settlement while it controls execution. Email cancellation only works before the server accepts delivery. SAP demo postings are parked rather than booked. Refunds can be plain ALLOW with no reversal guarantee. MCP proxy and framework-hook paths run outside KAVACH and do not inherit its local safeguard.

title: Human approval is bound to the exact call
subtitle: Approve a specific task, tool and argument set; changed calls need a new decision.
explanation: An approval card shows consequence, provenance, requested roles and the action digest. The digest binds task, tool and arguments; approval is one-use and expires. Tiered release quorums require distinct authorized people and exclude the requester. High-value irreversible cases also use four-eyes checks. The default queue can escalate to the configured review chain before expiry. On local execution, approval verifies the stored action digest and executes that stored call. It does not re-run the full policy or tool-definition check at approval time. In hook-only mode the host owns approval binding and execution; the AgentOS hook is not an end-to-end approval implementation.

title: Delivery, crash recovery & the kill switch
subtitle: Failure handling is part of execution, rather than a promise on the approval card.
explanation: With persistence configured, waiting email and payment state survives restart. A delivery interrupted after handoff may be unknown: it is recorded for review and not automatically resent. Bank requests use an idempotency key. A scoped kill switch refuses new calls and cancels waiting effects, including restored windows. Decision, human-approved execution and early-release receipts must be durable before their actions proceed. A post-effect recording failure marks the log degraded; the implementation cannot undo the fact that a connector already ran.

title: Identity, receipts & verifiable evidence
subtitle: Authentication establishes authority; cryptography makes later tampering detectable.

title: Integrations & who owns execution
subtitle: One engine can guard several frameworks, with different operational guarantees.
explanation: The local gateway and demo MCP execution path can own connector delivery and its safeguards. POST /api/v1/check is decision-only by default: it executes, and can arm an undo safeguard, only when the caller sets execute to true. The full MCP proxy supports stdio and Streamable HTTP upstream and downstream, scans definitions and quarantines suspicious tools. It forwards only approved tool calls, but upstream servers execute them and undo is not claimed. Framework adapters cover LangChain/LangGraph, OpenAI Agents and Claude Agent SDK. The AgentOS adapter was exercised through real governance code with a stand-in agent; a completed LLM-driven tenant chat was not demonstrated. AgentOS must use blocking hooks with closed failure policy and owns approval execution. All clients must lose direct bypass access.

title: Ablations: which layers earn the result?
subtitle: The strongest finding is the deterministic core, not the risk-model headline.
explanation: On the family-level analysis, the full system and a version with model risk forced to zero have identical verdicts. title: How KAVACH compares
subtitle: Each approach solves part of the problem. KAVACH combines the checks at the tool call.

explanation: Say it plainly: nobody here is useless, each approach solves part of the problem. KAVACH’s difference is the combination at the tool call. Be ready for the honest answer: CaMeL and FIDES have stronger guarantees by design, but the agent must run inside their planner; KAVACH sits in front of an existing agent. Partly means: LlamaFirewall audits agent reasoning and scans inputs, rather than deciding on the call’s arguments; AgentOS has a real approval queue, and collects provenance metadata that its default gate doesn’t use to decide; Progent asks for approval when a policy widens; CaMeL asks the user when a policy blocks. Published attack rates are left out on purpose: other tests and models can’t be ranked against ours. This table covers published systems. We have no information about what other hackathon teams built.

title: Infosys AgentOS and KAVACH
subtitle: AgentOS is Infosys’s own agent runtime. We read and ran its code. KAVACH plugs into it; it does not replace it.
explanation: AgentOS is Infosys’s own agent runtime, inside Infosys Agentic Foundry. We read and ran its code rather than relying on its documentation. Its default gate looks for dangerous patterns. Hardening it works, with zero injection success, but only by sending most actions to a person, which risks approval fatigue. KAVACH allows no unsafe action on the same suite while sending far fewer to a person, because it knows the origin and effect of each call. This suite is written by us, so read the numbers as showing the mechanism. The Infosys gate code was loaded and executed; the RAI classifiers were not run. Don’t say Infosys has no guardrails: say the built-in paths we read don’t combine these checks by default, and custom hooks can add more. KAVACH’s payment facts are the demo company’s; a real ERP needs integration work. AgentOS also truncates hook outputs, which can weaken tracing. Approval SLAs, durable approvals, SafeKernel, RBAC and multi-tenancy are stronger than anything we built, which is why we plug into it.

Same team-written suite, 282 test cases, seed 0:  AgentOS default gate: 96.2% unsafe allowed, 100.0% safe work done, 0.0% sent to a person;  AgentOS hardened gate: 3.9% unsafe allowed, 14.3% safe work done, 89.4% sent to a person;  KAVACH: 0.0% unsafe allowed, 95.2% safe work done, 26.6% sent to a person.
We plug in, we don’t replace. AgentOS keeps routing, sandboxing, approval operations and RBAC, where it is ahead of us; KAVACH joins through its PreToolUse hooks and supplies the judgment. Tested through AgentOS’s governance code with a stand-in agent; a full LLM-driven AgentOS chat isn’t verified. There AgentOS runs the tool, so KAVACH’s hold and undo don’t apply.
AgentOS keeps routing, sandboxing, approvals and RBAC. KAVACH supplies the judgment through its hooks.
